title: The Dragon Who Loved Snowflakes
markdown:
Witch Mabli’s boots crunched on the packed snow. Glacialift’s air was so crisp it felt like biting an icicle. Beside her, Wisp, a snow hare the colour of a winter storm, hopped along. His ears twitched like nervous antennae. His nose was a constant sniff-and-explore device. They were here to judge the Festival of Frosty Feats. Mabli, practical as ever, agreed for the prize money. It would finally fix her leaky cauldron.

Glacialift was a dizzying, delightful marvel. Frozen roads snaked up the mountain like icy serpents. High in the thin air, markets shimmered under ice arches. Wool banners snapped like tiny flags, shouting about frozen feats. The air smelled of roasting nuts and something acrid, like burnt sugar or a dragon’s sneeze. “Quite the spectacle, isn’t it, Wisp?” Mabli murmured. Ice sculptors carved frost-breathing beasts. Fire dancers swirled controlled flames. A man with a red nose juggled frozen fish that thumped with each catch.

Then they saw him. A creature of immense scale and shimmering obsidian scales. Ignis, a dragon. He wasn’t roaring or breathing fire. He was carefully, painstakingly, building an ice sculpture of a tiny, delicate snowflake. His movements were slow, deliberate, almost fragile. It was odd. Like a thundercloud trying to knit.

Mabli, who noticed the smallest wobble in a broomstick, tilted her head. “Interesting medium for a dragon, wouldn’t you agree, Wisp?” she said dryly. Wisp was busy trying to reassemble a discarded gingerbread man with enthusiastic licks. “And such intricate work. One might worry about accidental fumigations, given the… general volcanic nature of your species.”

Ignis’s colossal head snapped up. His voice was a low rumble that vibrated in Mabli’s bones. “Accidental fumigations? Madam Witch, my control is impeccable. This snowflake,” he declared, puffing out his chest and sending icicles raining down, “represents the transient beauty of winter. A delicate art, not for the heavy-handed or the unobservant.” His wings gave a nervous flutter.

Mabli blinked. “Oh, I didn’t doubt your control, Ignis. Not at all. More that a creature of your stature, with your magnificent fire-breathing, might melt it with a casual sigh. It’s just very *small*.”

Uh oh. Mabli had just stepped on a particularly sensitive dragon toe. Ignis visibly deflated. His scales dimmed. He turned away, his tail sweeping snow into a miniature avalanche. “Small?” His voice was a wounded whisper. “You find my dedication to detail… small?”

Wisp nudged Mabli. “He looks sad, Mabli. Like when I lost my favourite dandelion puff. His sparkle is gone.”

Mabli sighed. She wasn’t a diplomat for sensitive dragons. “It’s not small in skill, Ignis,” she tried. Her voice was still too blunt. “It’s small in *scale*. Most dragons sculpt mountains. Not… frost flowers. It’s impressive, of course, but… unexpected.” The words hung in the air. The festival continued. Ignis performed with less grandeur. His pride was bruised, like a cracked ice crystal.

The final event was the ‘Flight of Fancy.’ Ignis was supposed to perform an aerial ballet. But his heart wasn’t in it. He soared, his wings beating powerfully. But his movements were jerky. He nearly collided with a towering icicle spire shaped like a stoic mountain troll. Chunks of ice rained down near the spectators. The crowd gasped.

Wisp squeaked on Mabli’s shoulder, clutching her cloak. “He’s still thinking about the snowflake, Mabli! His feelings are all jumbled up. He's not flying with his chest, he's flying with his hurt feelings!”

Mabli saw the unintentional chaos. She felt a pang of responsibility. It wasn't about her leaky cauldron anymore. This was about a magnificent creature in distress. She scrambled down from her judging seat. Wisp guided her through the crowd. “Ignis!” she called. Her voice carried. “Ignis, if you are going to be mysterious, you could at least be punctual with your near-disasters!”

The dragon faltered. His grand loop turned into a wobbly circle. Slowly, with a rumble that shook snow from nearby stalls, he descended. He landed gently. He looked magnificent, but forlorn. His golden eyes held deep sadness.

“I… I apologize,” Mabli began, feeling awkward. She wasn’t used to apologizing to dragons. “My observation about the snowflake was… blunt. Perhaps too blunt for an artist of your calibre. I meant it was impressive *because* it was so detailed, so intricate, so unlike the grand gestures one often sees from creatures of your magnitude. It was a testament to your incredible control.” She gestured to Wisp, who hopped forward. “He noticed,” Mabli continued, her voice softening. “He saw your feelings were hurt. I was so focused on the *why*, the practicalities, I forgot to appreciate the *how*. The sheer beauty of your delicate craft.”

Wisp nudged Ignis’s colossal, sapphire-blue toe. “It was the prettiest snowflake,” he squeaked. His voice was clear. “And your sky-dancing was almost as good as a good chase after a runaway cheese roll, which is very, very good.”

Ignis looked from Mabli to Wisp. His great golden eyes widened. Surprise. Wonder. He hadn’t expected an apology. Not from a witch who looked like she’d rather be brewing potions. Not from a small witch and an even smaller hare. The sheer unexpectedness of it all melted something deep within him. A frozen knot of pride and misunderstanding.

A low, rumbling chuckle echoed through Glacialift. It was free of hurt, tinged with amusement. “You see,” Ignis said, his voice majestic again, but warm, “even dragons have their… artistic sensitivities. And their… rather keen judges, it seems.” He nudged Mabli gently with his snout. The crowd had gathered. They witnessed this extraordinary moment.

By the end of the festival, the official judges, a stern-faced gnome and a perpetually flustered yeti, were in an uproar. The ice sculptures were good. The fire dancers dazzling. But the real story? The dragon who learned to fly with his heart. The witch who learned to speak to it. Mabli and Ignis, an unlikely pair. They were declared joint honorary judges for life. Mabli smiled. Her cauldron would be fixed. She’d gained something far more valuable. A very unusual, very dignified, and surprisingly sensitive friend. A friend who, she suspected, might occasionally need help with his delicate artistic endeavours.
characters: witch Mabli, snow hare Wisp, a dragon who is trying to seem dignified
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
